{{Short description|Theorem concerning uniform convergence}}
In [[measure theory]], an area of [[mathematics]], '''Egorov's theorem''' establishes a condition for the [[uniform convergence]] of a [[pointwise convergence|pointwise convergent]] [[sequence]] of [[measurable function]]s. It is also named '''Severini–Egoroff theorem''' or '''Severini–Egorov theorem''', after [[Carlo Severini]], an [[Italia]]n [[mathematician]], and [[Dmitri Egorov]], a [[Russia]]n mathematician and [[geometer]], who published independent proofs respectively in 1910 and 1911.

Egorov's theorem can be used along with [[support (mathematics)|compactly supported]] [[continuous function]]s to prove [[Lusin's theorem]] for [[integrable function]]s.

==Historical note==
The first proof of the theorem was given by [[Carlo Severini]] in 1910:<ref>Published in {{Harv|Severini|1910|pp=3–4}}.</ref><ref>According to {{Harvtxt|Straneo|1952|p=101}}, Severini, while acknowledging his own priority in the publication of the result, was unwilling to disclose it publicly: it was [[Leonida Tonelli]] who, in the note {{Harv|Tonelli|1924}}, credited him the priority for the first time.</ref> he used the result as a tool in his research on [[Series (mathematics)|series]] of [[orthogonal functions]]. His work remained apparently unnoticed outside [[Italy]], probably due to the fact that it is written in [[Italian language|Italian]], appeared in a scientific journal with limited diffusion and was considered only as a means to obtain other theorems. A year later [[Dmitri Egorov]] published his independently proved results,<ref>In the note {{Harv|Egoroff|1911}}.</ref> and the theorem became widely known under his name: however, it is not uncommon to find references to this theorem as the Severini–Egoroff theorem. The first mathematicians to prove independently the theorem in the nowadays common abstract [[measure space]] setting were {{Harvs|txt|first=Frigyes|last=Riesz|author-link=Frigyes Riesz|year=1922|year2=1928}}, and in {{Harvs|txt|first=Wacław|last=Sierpiński|author-link=Wacław Sierpiński|year=1928}}:<ref>According to {{Harvtxt|Cafiero|1959|p=315}} and {{Harvtxt|Saks|1937|p=17}}.</ref> an earlier generalization is due to [[Nikolai Luzin]], who succeeded in slightly relaxing the requirement of finiteness of measure of the [[Domain of a function|domain]] of convergence of the [[Pointwise convergence|pointwise converging functions]] in the long (242 pages) paper {{Harv|Luzin|1916}}.<ref>According to {{Harvtxt|Saks|1937|p=19}}.</ref> Further generalizations were given much later by [[Pavel Korovkin]], in the paper {{Harv|Korovkin|1947}}, and by [[Gabriel Mokobodzki]] in the paper {{Harv|Mokobodzki|1970}}: in particular Korovkin extended the result to a class of non–negative [[set function]]s more general than measures.<ref>See {{Harvtxt|Korovkin|1947|pp=1265–266}} and its [https://zbmath.org/?format=complete&q=an:0038.03803 zbMath review by G. Hajós]: the reviewer notes that this class contains the transfinite diameter of [[Euclidean plane|plane set]]s belonging to <math>\Bbb C</math>.</ref>

==Formal statement and proof==
===Statement===
Let <math>(f_n)</math> be a sequence of <math>M</math>-valued measurable functions, where <math>M</math> is a separable metric space, on some [[measure space]] <math>(X,\sigma,\mu)</math>, and suppose there is a [[measurable set|measurable subset]] <math>A \subseteq X</math>, with finite <math>\mu</math>-measure, such that  <math>(f_n)</math> [[limit of a sequence|converges]] <math>\mu</math>-[[almost everywhere]] on <math>A</math> to a limit function <math>f</math>. The following result holds: for every <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, there exists a measurable [[subset]] <math>B</math> of <math>A</math> such that <math>\mu (B)<\varepsilon</math>, and <math>(f_n)</math> [[uniform convergence|converges to <math>f</math> uniformly]] on <math>A\setminus B</math>.

Here, <math>\mu (B)</math> denotes the <math>\mu</math>-measure of <math>B</math>. In words, the theorem says that pointwise convergence almost everywhere on <math>A</math> implies the apparently much stronger uniform convergence everywhere except on some subset <math>B</math> of arbitrarily small measure. This type of convergence is called ''almost uniform convergence''.

===Discussion of assumptions and a counterexample===
* The hypothesis <math>\mu (A)<\infty</math> is necessary. To see this, it is simple to construct a counterexample when μ is the [[Lebesgue measure]]: consider the sequence of real-valued [[indicator function]]s <math display="block">f_n(x) = 1_{[n,n+1]}(x), \qquad n\in\N,\ x\in\R,</math> defined on the [[real line]]. This sequence converges pointwise to the zero function everywhere but does not converge uniformly on <math>\R\setminus B</math> for any set <math>B</math> of finite measure: a counterexample in the general [[Dimension|<math>n</math>-dimensional]] [[real vector space]] <math>\R^n</math> can be constructed as shown by {{Harvtxt|Cafiero|1959|p=302}}.
* The separability of the metric space is needed to make sure that for <math>M</math>-valued, measurable functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>, the distance <math>d(f(x), g(x))</math> is again a measurable real-valued function of <math>x</math>.

===Proof===
Fix <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>.
For natural numbers ''n'' and ''k'', define the set ''E<sub>n,k</sub>'' by the [[union (set theory)|union]]

<math display=block> E_{n,k} = \bigcup_{m\ge n} \left\{ x\in A \,\Big|\, |f_m(x) - f(x)| \ge \frac1k \right\}.</math>

These sets get smaller as ''n'' increases, meaning that ''E''<sub>''n''+1,''k''</sub> is always a subset of ''E<sub>n,k</sub>'', because the first union involves fewer sets. A point ''x'', for which the sequence (''f<sub>m</sub>''(''x'')) converges to ''f''(''x''), cannot be in every ''E<sub>n,k</sub>'' for a fixed ''k'', because ''f<sub>m</sub>''(''x'') has to stay closer to ''f''(''x'') than 1/''k'' eventually. Hence by the assumption of μ-almost everywhere pointwise convergence on ''A'',

<math display=block>\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\N}E_{n,k}\right)=0</math>

for every ''k''. Since ''A'' is of finite measure, we have [[Measure (mathematics)#Continuity_from_above|continuity from above]]; hence there exists, for each ''k'', some natural number ''n<sub>k</sub>'' such that

<math display=block>\mu(E_{n_k,k}) < \frac\varepsilon{2^k}.</math>

For ''x'' in this set we consider the speed of approach into the 1/''k''-[[neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of ''f''(''x'') as too slow. Define

<math display=block>B = \bigcup_{k\in\N} E_{n_k,k}</math>

as the set of all those points ''x'' in ''A'', for which the speed of approach into ''at least one'' of these 1/''k''-neighbourhoods of ''f''(''x'') is too slow. On the set difference <math> A\setminus B</math> we therefore have uniform convergence. Explicitly, for any <math>\epsilon</math>, let <math>\frac 1 k < \epsilon</math>, then for any <math>n > n_k</math>, we have <math>|f_n - f| < \epsilon</math> on all of <math> A\setminus B</math>.

Appealing to the [[sigma additivity]] of μ and using the [[geometric series]], we get

<math display=block>\mu(B) \le \sum_{k\in\N} \mu(E_{n_k,k}) < \sum_{k\in\N}\frac\varepsilon{2^k}=\varepsilon.</math>

==Generalizations==
===Luzin's version===
{{main|Lusin's theorem}}
[[Nikolai Luzin]]'s generalization of the Severini–Egorov theorem is presented here according to {{Harvtxt|Saks|1937|p=19}}.

====Statement====
Under the same hypothesis of the abstract Severini–Egorov theorem suppose that ''A'' is the [[union (set theory)|union]] of a [[sequence]] of [[measurable set]]s of finite μ-measure, and (''f<sub>n</sub>'') is a given sequence of ''M''-valued measurable functions on some [[measure space]] (''X'',Σ,μ), such that (''f''<sub>''n''</sub>) [[limit of a sequence|converges]] μ-[[almost everywhere]] on ''A'' to a limit function ''f'', then ''A'' can be expressed as the union of a sequence of measurable sets ''H'', ''A<sub>1</sub>'', ''A<sub>2</sub>'',... such that μ(''H'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 and (''f<sub>n</sub>'') converges to ''f'' uniformly on each set ''A<sub>k</sub>''.

====Proof====
It is sufficient to consider the case in which the set ''A'' is itself of finite μ-measure: using this hypothesis and the standard Severini–Egorov theorem, it is possible to define by [[mathematical induction]] a sequence of sets {''A<sub>k</sub>''}<sub>k=1,2,...</sub> such that

<math display=block>\mu\left (A \setminus \bigcup_{k=1}^{N} A_k \right)\leq\frac{1}{N}</math>

and such that (''f<sub>n</sub>'') converges to ''f'' uniformly on each set ''A<sub>k</sub>'' for each ''k''. Choosing

<math display=block>H=A\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k</math>

then obviously μ(''H'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 and the theorem is proved.

===Korovkin's version===
The proof of the Korovkin version follows closely the version on {{Harvtxt|Kharazishvili|2000|pp=183–184}}, which however generalizes it to some extent by considering [[admissible functional]]s instead of [[Measure (mathematics)|non-negative measures]] and [[inequality (mathematics)|inequalities]] <math>\leq</math> and <math>\geq</math> respectively in conditions 1 and 2.

====Statement====
Let <math display=inline>(M,d)</math> denote a [[separable space|separable]] [[metric space]] and <math display=inline>(X,\Sigma )</math> a [[measurable space]]: consider a [[measurable set]] <math display=inline>A</math> and a [[Set (mathematics)|class]] <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> containing <math display=inline>A</math> and its measurable [[subset]]s such that their [[countable]] in [[Union (set theory)|unions]] and [[Intersection (set theory)|intersections]] belong to the same class. Suppose there exists a [[Measure (mathematics)|non-negative measure]] <math display=inline>\mu</math> such that <math display=inline>\mu(A)</math> exists and
# <math>\mu(\cap A_n) = \lim \mu(A_n)</math> if <math>A_1 \supset A_2 \supset \cdots</math> with <math>A_n\in\mathfrak{A}</math> for all <math display=inline>n</math>
# <math>\mu(\cup A_n) = \lim \mu(A_n)</math> if <math>A_1 \subset A_2 \subset \cdots</math> with <math>\cup A_n\in\mathfrak{A}</math>.
If <math display=inline>f_n</math> is a sequence of <math display=inline>M</math>-valued measurable functions [[limit of a sequence|converging]] <math display=inline>\mu</math>-[[almost everywhere]] on <math display=inline>A\in\mathfrak{A}</math> to a limit function <math display=inline>f</math>, then there exists a [[subset]] <math display=inline>A^\prime</math> of <math display=inline>A</math> such that <math display=inline>0<\mu (A)-\mu(A^\prime)<\varepsilon </math>0 and where the convergence is also uniform.

====Proof====
Consider the [[Indexed family|indexed family of sets]] whose [[index set]] is the set of [[natural number]]s <math>m\in\N,</math> defined as follows:

<math display=block>A_{0,m}=\left\{x\in A|d(f_n(x),f(x)) \le 1\ \forall n\geq m\right\}</math>

Obviously

<math display=block>A_{0,1}\subseteq A_{0,2}\subseteq A_{0,3}\subseteq\dots</math>

and

<math display=block>A=\bigcup_{m\in\N}A_{0,m}</math>

therefore there is a [[natural number]] ''m<sub>0</sub>'' such that putting ''A<sub>0,m<sub>0</sub></sub>''=''A<sub>0</sub>'' the following relation holds true:

<math display=block>0\leq\mu(A)-\mu(A_0)\leq\varepsilon</math>

Using ''A<sub>0</sub>'' it is possible to define the following indexed family

<math display=block>A_{1,m}=\left\{x\in A_0\left| d(f_m(x),f(x)) \le \frac12 \ \forall n\geq m\right.\right\}</math>

satisfying the following two relationships, analogous to the previously found ones, i.e.

<math display=block>A_{1,1}\subseteq A_{1,2}\subseteq A_{1,3}\subseteq\dots</math>

and

<math display=block>A_0=\bigcup_{m\in\N}A_{1,m}</math>

This fact enable us to define the set ''A<sub>1,m<sub>1</sub></sub>''=''A<sub>1</sub>'', where ''m<sub>1</sub>'' is a surely existing natural number such that

<math display=block>0\leq\mu(A)-\mu(A_1)\leq\varepsilon</math>

By iterating the shown construction, another indexed family of set {''A<sub>n</sub>''} is defined such that it has the following properties:

* <math>A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq A_2\supseteq\cdots</math>
* <math>0\leq\mu(A)-\mu(A_m)\leq\varepsilon</math> for all <math>m\in\N</math>
* for each <math>m\in\N</math> there exists ''k<sub>m</sub>'' such that for all <math>n \geq k_m</math> then <math>d(f_n(x),f(x)) \le 2^{-m}</math> for all <math>x \in A_m</math>

and finally putting

<math display=block>A'=\bigcup_{n\in\N}A_n</math>

the thesis is easily proved.
